title: Marginal cost

definition.text: The extra total cost of producing one more unit of output.

facts.text: It differs from average cost, which is total cost divided by the number of units made.
It counts only costs that change with output: for one more car, the labour and parts, but not the factory building.
Because fixed costs do not change with output, doubling them leaves marginal cost, and the profit-maximizing price and quantity, unchanged.
In the short run it eventually rises, as more labour and materials press against a fixed building and machinery.
A competitive firm keeps producing as long as the sale price exceeds the marginal cost, stopping where the two are equal.
The marginal cost curve crosses the average total cost and average variable cost curves at their lowest points.
With economies of scale, pricing at marginal cost fails to cover total costs and so needs a subsidy.
In a survey of 200 executives, 11% said their marginal costs rose with output, 48% said they were constant and 41% said they fell.

contested_note: Textbook models assume marginal cost rises with output, but many empirical studies find it constant or falling for most firms.

title: Marginal social cost
article: Marginal cost#Private versus social marginal cost

definition.text: The full cost to society of producing one more unit: the producer's own cost plus any cost or benefit falling on people outside the sale.

facts.text: Marginal private cost is the cost the firm itself bears, and it is the one businesses use when maximizing profit.
Examples are air pollution harming third parties and flu shots protecting others from infection.
When social cost exceeds private cost, as with polluting production, there is a negative externality and the market overproduces the good.
Firms create such externalities by pushing part of their costs onto third parties to cut their own costs.
When social cost is below private cost, as with education, there is a positive externality and the market underproduces.

definition.text: A market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service.

facts.text: A monopoly lacks competition and close substitutes, so it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits.
Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market.
Monopolies get their power from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate.
A monopolist picks the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, aiming at the largest total profit rather than the highest price.
Compared with perfect competition it sells less at a higher price, and the trades it forgoes create a deadweight loss.
Contestable-market theory says a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low.
Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behaviour.
The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses.

title: Natural monopoly

definition.text: A firm whose average cost of production keeps falling across the whole range of market demand, so one large supplier is cheaper than several small ones.

facts.text: Such markets, left alone, tend to turn into a monopoly, often after an early entrant expands fast and drives out rivals.
J.S. Mill first called monopolies 'natural' in 1848, citing gas and water supply, roads, canals and railways.
Breaking them up is inefficient by definition, so governments mostly use regulation and public ownership.
Regulators often impose average-cost pricing, which removes excess profit but weakens the incentive to cut costs.

notes: A page 'Natural monopoly' is also crawled; the merge may prefer it.

definition.text: A monopoly created when a government gives one person or company the exclusive right to supply something.

facts.text: It can be granted by a law that excludes rivals, or indirectly through patents, trademarks and copyright.
States grant them to reward risky investment or to enrich a domestic interest group.
A publisher can use its copyright monopoly to charge American students more than Ethiopian students for the same textbook.

definition.text: The rule that a monopoly's markup, as a share of its price, is inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand it faces.

facts.text: The markup is measured by the Lerner index: price minus marginal cost, divided by price, equals minus one over the elasticity of demand.
Perfectly competitive firms have zero market power and simply take the market price.
